records.name: Roraima
records.summary:
The national framework applies in Roraima with no documented state-level deviation: protections come from the federal supreme court — name and gender-marker change without surgery or court order, and the 2019 ruling equating anti-LGBT crimes with racism — rather than a comprehensive statute, and non-binary birth-certificate recognition is handled case-by-case state by state.

The country carries the world's highest absolute toll of killings of trans people, concentrated away from the capitals, and observers stress that protections are uneven in practice, thinning in the interior. The earlier specific claims for Roraima — no killings recorded for 2024, lowest national band for 2025 — lack a citation in this region's audited sources and are treated as unconfirmed; in so small a state a single case would dominate the statistics in any year, and official counts under-record.

For a visitor the picture is the national one with interior attenuation: rights on paper, thin services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility mechanism on record either.

records.name: Acre
records.summary:

The rest is the national picture with an interior discount: the country logs the world's highest absolute number of killings of trans people, weighted away from the capitals; protections are uneven in practice; and Acre is among the least populous units, so any recorded count — including the earlier claim of zero killings in 2024, which this packet's audited sources do not carry — is statistically fragile and under-recorded.

A current-status check confirms the federal framework (marriage equality since 2013, no criminalisation, nationwide document rectification) unchanged. No state-level hostility mechanism is on record.

records.name: Tocantins
records.summary:
Tocantins stands entirely under Brazil's nationally uniform framework: marriage equality since 2013, name and gender-marker change at the registry without surgery since 2018, homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism by the Supreme Court in 2019, and non-binary civil-registry amendments allowed by a 2025 superior-court ruling — protections built by the courts rather than statute, with repeal efforts active in Congress bearing on their stability.

No Tocantins-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement pattern is on file. A Brazilian law-firm guide records that the legal rights are identical nationwide while major cities are broadly welcoming and smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction — a distinction that reaches through Tocantins as elsewhere.

Brazil continues to have one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people; that national profile, not any local divergence, sets the state's risk. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing political visibility at local level nationally.
